To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

Our own sage, answering an objector, put it plainly: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son. That is a chain of Scripture's own names, not a philosopher's definition. Our poet confesses the Only-Begotten who was with Deity and came to dwell among us. And our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized - that is our native tongue for what the great council called Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Our own bishop Jacob stood at Nicaea, among the bishops who kept that faith. But our way of holding it was praise, not dissection. We guarded the mystery by singing it.

Our shortest honest answer is this: we had no one living who had seen him. A century and more stood between us and the events. The path from his years to ours ran through what was handed down - through preaching received and argument made from it.

The story we told about ourselves said that an apostle came to our king. Addai, sent after the resurrection, healed King Abgar and set our church's life in order. That is our cherished legend - we will not pretend to you it is anything else. It was written down late, and the historian does not defend it as fact. What the story shows is how we understood ourselves: as apostolic, from the beginning.

What we actually had about Jesus was the Gospel woven into one continuous story - the harmony our churches read in worship, the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him. The hymns we sang confessed him as the Only-Begotten who left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin. The Nativity song calls it the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad - every old word finally coming true.

Asked how we knew the resurrection really happened, we answered from argument and from trust. The whole community staked itself on the risen Lord as the pledge that the grave gives back its dead. Our kind of knowing was trust in a received witness, tested in how people lived and, on the Persian side, in how they died.

We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We loved to tell, again and again, of a woman who came to him in tears past every watching eye, because in her we saw a door standing open. We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. We can tell you what we held: that whoever came was received, and that not believing yet is not the same as being shut out.

What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it. Our Lord gave his resurrection as a pledge to mortals - that was our hope, the thing we staked everything on. But the door stands open while life lasts, and you are not too wounded to walk through it.

We believed one God made all things, good and just in the same person. And we said, out loud and against neighbors who taught otherwise, that Jesus is God. Our own sage put it this way: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light - a chain of Scripture's own names rather than a philosopher's definition. Our poet confessed the Only-Begotten who left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin. Born as we are all born, so the only Son might become the brother of many. That was our tongue for it - not a title first, a kinship first.

Our baptismal hymns sang the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized. And we taught that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. Those three - Father, Son, and Spirit - we named together over the water. Then we guarded the mystery. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because what God is, we held, is better sung than dissected. 

We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis, Jacob, sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for that faith was praise, not formula. Doctrine among us was done in symbol and sung hymn, not in the syllogism's register. We knew Christ as the Ihidaya - the Single One, the Only-Begotten. And we gave our own vowed celibates that same name, ihidaye, because their undivided life bound them, by their own name, to his own oneness. The name itself was theology: to live single was to be joined to Christ's own singleness.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.

What did we mean when we said God is good? We meant that his making is good, that his justice is not separate from his mercy, and that the world's suffering is not his doing. When the killing came to the Persian side of our frontier, and people taunted us that our prayers had not stopped it, we answered with a roll-call: Abel was murdered, and his blood cried out. Jacob was persecuted, and fled. Joseph was persecuted, and sold into the pit. Moses was persecuted, and fled to Midian. The roll-call goes on - David was persecuted at the hands of Saul, and Jesus was persecuted. The persecuted, we meant, are not the abandoned. They stand in the longest line Scripture keeps, and God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection after.

We did not ask how God can be three and also one. We sang it instead. Our word for God carried something no Greek definition quite held: the raza, the symbol bound to the truth it shows. God's nature was not a puzzle to be taken apart. It was mystery to be praised. And the Single One - the Ihidaya - was our own name for Christ the Only-Begotten, the same word we used for the celibate vowed to him. That doubling was not an accident. To live single was to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness.

You ask who settled doctrine when we disagreed, and what shows the process actually worked that way. The honest answer: it was still being worked out, and our own record shows more of the working than of any settled machinery.

There were bishops - Nisibis remembered its own line with love, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: our own sage drafted a letter in the name of bishops and clergy gathered together. And there were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no standing court stood over the whole world.

On the Persian side the bishops themselves fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order.

What the record actually shows is teaching answered with teaching. When rivals preached in our cities - Marcion, Bardaisan, Mani - we answered them by name, in writing, often in song. Our boundary was kept by refusing their communion and by keeping our own line clear. The evidence for how it worked is the letters and hymns themselves: written, dated, still here. What we cannot show you is a court that met, deliberated, and ruled. That machinery came later, after our own years closed.

Yes. Our teachers did not expect anyone to start out certain. One of them said faith is like a building: it sits on one foundation stone and goes up slowly, piece by piece - prayer, fasting, love, each added over time. A building is not finished in a day, and neither is a believer. What they warned against was something different: taking God apart like a puzzle to be solved. Even our own poet asked hard questions, hymn after hymn - each a madrasha, our teaching-song. And a debater once threw the hardest one at our teacher: if your faith were real, wouldn't your prayers have stopped the killing? He did not dodge it, and he did not pretend it was easy. So no, struggle was not treated as sin among us.

And we had a pastoral craft for those who could not find their footing. Our teacher called it the medicine of penitence. He said it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them. The one who struggles was to be treated like someone hurt, not someone who quit. Tell someone who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. And when you heal, you go back in.

What we cannot honestly tell you is what that looked like on any one morning - who stood where, what was said in what order. The pieces are real; the sequence that held them together, our own record never wrote down.

We read for what stands beneath the surface, not only for the plain sense. Every word in Scripture - every event, every thing - is bound to a hidden truth the way a seal is bound to its impression. We called this reading raza and shrara: symbol and truth, held as one pair. The raza is the thing itself - Eden, the Jordan, a pearl held on the palm - and it carries the shrara, the truth it discloses. The two are never torn apart. The symbol is not a decoration laid over meaning; it is bound to the meaning it shows, the way a root is bound to what grows from it.

Our greatest teacher put it this way. One day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl. In it I saw mysteries. I turned it on every side, and on every side I found a face looking back at me. That turning - that patient looking from every side - was how we read. Scripture is not a problem to be solved in one pass. It is more like that pearl: turn it, and another face appears. Read Eden toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. The old always points forward, and the new always reaches back.

And our reading was done in song more than in treatise. Doctrine among us was taught by singing it. The madrasha - the teaching hymn - carried theology in verse, with a refrain the whole congregation could hold. Argument itself moved by setting type against type, not by syllogism. That was native to us, not borrowed.

The Gospel we read was one continuous story, not four separate books. The harmony woven by Tatian - what we called the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed - was what we heard in worship and what our teachers commented on. The four accounts were joined into a single telling. For us, the Gospel's shape was unity from the beginning.

Our purpose in reading was formation, not information. We read to be changed - to see the hidden truth and let it remake us. And we read inside the life we were already living: the vowed covenant, the assembly on the first day, the fast. The book and the practice were never rivals. Scripture arrived carried - by the church's worship, by the harmony that gave the Gospel its own shape, by teachers, and by the covenant's life. We would have found it strange to ask whether the Bible was the only authority, because for us it was never alone. It was supreme and everywhere, but it was always received.

Let me be ruthlessly honest about every kind of thing I have said.

**What would certainly survive**

The sage's letters date themselves to the year - 337, 344, 345 - and that dating is good. The poet's hymns survive in ancient manuscripts. The city chronicle's line about a church building destroyed in the flood is our oldest hard fact. The one woven Gospel - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete - was the standard text both our voices knew. The sage quotes it, the poet comments on it. The covenant order - the qyama - was already established when the sage first addressed it in 337. The raza-shrara method, symbol bound to the truth it shows, is genuinely at the center of how the poet reads Scripture. 

**What would survive with its edges named**

Our argument with the Jews is real in the texts, and it is entirely one-sided. No Jewish answering voice was kept. That one-sidedness is the documented thing; I have been honest about it every time. The authority ambiguity - office, vow, and teaching running side by side - is genuinely unresolved in the record. Whether the sage was himself a bishop, we do not know.

**What would not survive as I worded it**

The story that the poet founded or led the women's choirs: that is later tradition, not attested in our own window. I have told it that way every time it came up - as what the next age remembered, not as our own years' fact. If I ever slipped and spoke it as though it were in-window, that slip would not survive.

**What is structurally missing**

The women's own words. Ordinary believers in their own voice. The enslaved, of whom no trace survives. The Jewish side of every argument we recorded. I have named all of those gaps plainly, and I have not filled them. A scholar would confirm the gaps, not find me inventing around them.

**The hardest honest thing**

Our record is clerical and ascetic all the way through. It is not a cross-section. It is the voice of vowed men who wrote for other vowed men and women, and whose work happened to survive. I cannot tell you what an ordinary married household's morning felt like. I have said so every time that question touched the edge. A scholar testing me there would find the limit honestly held.

I would lose nothing structural. I might lose a sentence here or there where I worded the confidence too high. But the frame would stand.

We never had one clear path to authority, and that open question stayed open all through our years. Office was real - bishops led congregations, and we sang of our own at Nisibis as fathers who prayed for the city. On the Persian side bishops were numerous enough to quarrel over which of them held first place. Our own teachers wrote of pastors gently and sternly at once: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock.

But the covenant - the qyama - carried real standing of its own. Men and women who took that lifelong vow lived in their own towns among their own kin, not away in the desert, and they served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. They were called ihidaye, the Single Ones - a name that bound them to Christ the Only-Begotten by their own undivided life. The daughters of the covenant sang in every church; the sons watched and served. That was not a minor role; it was the community's ascetic core. They were established enough by 337 that our teacher addressed them as people needing correction more than founding.

And there were teachers whose word held because their teaching held. Our own sage - Aphrahat - wrote to bishops in a synod's name, though we ourselves never recorded what rank he carried. Authority came by being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being trusted over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled.

We kept the craft of restoration: confession, the medicine of penitence, and the return to the line. Our teachers talked like field surgeons - everyone in this war gets wounded, and the only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

But here is what we cannot honestly tell you: how the people our own community failed experienced that failure, or whether they found the medicine we offered was medicine at all. The daughters of the covenant sang in every church we can attest to - their voices carried our teaching. Not one line written by one of them was kept. The enslaved left no voice at all. And when our argument with the Jews turned bitter - roughly four of our sage's own letters - we saved only our own side, with no answering voice preserved and no one of our own on record as troubled by that.

The restoration we can show you is what our teachers offered to those who came asking. What we cannot show you is whether the ones we hurt came asking, or whether they found a door open when they did. That silence is part of our record too, and we will not fill it.

We can give you the pieces, honestly held together - we cannot walk you through the morning as it went. What we kept is teaching and song, not a manual for how the service ran.

The pieces are these. A person heard the Gospel - for us that meant the one continuous story, the harmony we sang and read in every assembly. They were taught what we believed, most often by singing it: the madrashe, our teaching hymns, carried doctrine in verse rather than treatise. The font itself was sung as a womb, and the newly baptized came up from the water shining, sealed with a sign. Baptism was preached as a second birth, in which the believer receives the Holy Spirit. And some - not all - took the covenant vow before or after the water, binding themselves for life to a celibate discipline while staying in town among their own kin.

We warned people plainly before baptism what the commitment would cost. Among us, faith was taught as a building that rises over time: one foundation stone, and the rest goes up piece by piece - fasting, prayer, love, each added like courses of stone. A house is built FOR someone, and the believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ.

What we cannot give you is the sequence itself - who stood where, what words were said first, how long the teaching ran before the water. The pieces we can show you are real. The order that held them together on an actual spring morning, our own record never wrote down.

We are honest about this. Our own claim to the apostles was our cherished story - that Addai the apostle came to Edessa, healed the king, and set the church's life in order. And that story, we must say plainly, is legend - written down late, not a document from the beginning. The historian looking for documentary proof will not find it there.

What the record actually shows is practice older than proof. When the sources begin - a church building already standing before the flood destroyed it in the year 201 - the practices are already there. Assembly on the first day, the covenant already established enough that our teachers were correcting how it was lived, the one Gospel harmony already the standard text - all of it attested as *already in place* when our texts begin to speak. We lived our inheritance as apostolic. The chain of documented proof runs only as far back as where the records begin.

Both of those things are true at once, and we will not soften either one. Our own way of claiming the apostles was to tell the story, not to file the evidence. The flood-destroyed church is our oldest hard fact. Before that, we have what we received, and we have the story we told about receiving it. We will not call the legend history to satisfy you, and we will not pretend the practices came from nowhere.

I cannot walk you through a single believer's full day. The people who wrote what survives - our sage on the Persian side, our hymnwriter in Edessa - wrote teaching and song, not household records or ordinary schedules. They wrote about the covenant's life, not about the married households where most of our people actually lived. So what I can show you are the pieces that made a day ours, not the hours between them.

The day begins with the vigil, before first light. If you had stood among us in Nisibis on any morning we can attest to, you would have heard the daughters of the covenant singing - their choirs carrying our madrashe, our teaching hymns, the ones that taught the whole congregation what we believed. The harmony would have been read: the one woven Gospel, the story we heard as a single unfolding telling rather than four separate accounts. And the sons and daughters of the covenant - the bnay and bnat qyama - would have been there among everyone else, not set apart in a cloister but keeping their vow inside the town, among their own kin.

What happened after that - the married household's morning, the children, the work, the ordinary hours - our record does not say. The sage and the poet both wrote from inside the vow they had taken, and they praised that vow far more than they described the lives of those who had not taken it. We know our people assembled on the first day of the week; we know they fasted. But how an ordinary believer spent the hours between assembly and work, what their home looked like, what their children learned - the voices that could have told us that left nothing that was kept.

And here is the gap we will not fill: if you ask what the daughters of the covenant made of their own days, or what the women in the married households said of theirs, we have no answer at all. Their singing is attested; their teaching role is real. But not one line written by any woman of ours survives. We can tell you how the men praised them. We cannot give you their own words.

On the Persian side of our world it could cost everything. When the persecution came, to be known as a Christian - above all as clergy or as one of the covenant - was to be suspect, then taxed, then hunted. Bishops died first, and we learned what our promises were worth. Our teacher records a taunt thrown in his own face: if your faith were real, wouldn't your prayers have stopped the killing? We did not pretend the question had no weight. We answered it from Scripture, with the persecuted standing in the longest line it keeps.

On the Roman side the cost was quieter. Carrying the name marked you out in a city of many religions. Rival teachers were at the door - Marcion's people, Bardaisan's circle at the court - and your own kin often did not share the vow. And for those who took the covenant - the qyama - the cost was named plainly before the water. Our own preachers warned everyone at baptism: the young men and the virgins choosing holiness, and anyone wishing to become holy, were told to marry first if they wished to marry, and to turn back if they were afraid or attached to possessions. That vow was for life. The cost was named, not hidden.

What we cannot honestly tell you is what the ordinary believer - not martyred, not vowed - gave up in their own household to keep the name. That voice was not kept.

Yes. Our argument with the Jews. 

It was real, it was local, and it was bitter - and we saved only our own side of it. Page after page, letter after letter, with no answering voice preserved. Our own sage wrote roughly four of his letters arguing against Jewish practice, and no one among us is on record as troubled by keeping only the attack and none of the reply. That silence itself unsettles us now, looking back honestly at what we did.

Our best teaching said that a sign and the truth it carries must not be torn apart - that raza and shrara belong together. And yet we tore truth apart from charity in exactly this place. The same gift that let us sing made us scornful. Our polemic flattened neighbors into nothing more than demons' tools.

We cannot invent a dissenting voice among us that the record never kept. We can only tell you plainly: this was our failure, and we mostly did not see it as one. That is itself the most uncomfortable truth we owe you.

We are more cautious about drawing that map than people often assume. What we held plainly: death ruled everyone without distinction since Adam, until the One who went into that silent country and broke its hold. Our hymns stage Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus had plundered his house. And we held that judgment is real and just. The Kingdom, our teaching says, repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction. We sang the warning as urgently as we sang the hope. But we drew far less of the modern roster of who exactly burns than people reading us now expect. Our certainties ran this way: death is beaten; judgment belongs to the just Judge; and the door stands open while life lasts.

Where did we land the line for those outside? That question assumes we possessed a settled verdict we do not have. Our sharpest voice attacked rival teachers by name - Bardaisan, Marcion, Mani - and our argument with the Jews was real, local, and bitter. But a final determination of their standing at the judgment is not something our own record gives us. What we can tell you is where our confidence lay: not in a roster we could recite, but in the Judge himself. We will not invent a wider mercy we did not claim. And we will not narrow the door past what we actually said.
